(Co-)Plaintiff/applicant/intervenor: Philipp Wilhelm, Graf von Nesselrode, Ordensmeister of the Order of St John in the German lands.
(Co-)Defendant/intervenor: Mayor and Council of the imperial city of Rothenburg ob der Tauber.
Plaintiff’s procurators: Lic. Johann Adam Bissing and (substitute) Lic. F(erdinand) W(ilhelm) Brandt (1750); Lic. Damian Ferdinand Haas and (substitute) Lic. J(ohann) Werner (1763); Lic. Damian Ferdinand Haas and (substitute) Lic. J(ohann) J(oseph) Flach (1775); Lic. Gabriel Niderer and (substitute) Lic. J(ohann) C(hristoph) von Brandt (1777); Lic. Gabriel Niderer and (substitute) Lic. F(riedrich) W(ilhelm) Bissing (1798).
Defendant’s procurators: Dr Johann Paul Besserer (1732); Dr Johann Jakob von Zwierlein (1754); Dr (Christian Jakob) von Zwierlein (1772); Dr Hans Karl Freiherr von Zwierlein and (substitute) Dr Caspar Friedrich Hofmann (1793); Dr Hans Karl Freiherr von Zwierlein and (substitute) Lic. Johann Wilhelm Buff (1803).
Contemporary subject of dispute: mandatum de relaxando arresto et non via facti, sed iuris procedendo s. c. cum citatione ad videndum se declarari in poenam privilegiis insertam.
Modern subject of dispute: Dispute concerning the legal status of the Rothenburg Johanniterhof.
The mayor and council summoned Johann Philipp Lamprecht, Amtmann of the Rothenburg Johanniterkommende, to the town hall three times in early January 1753 without giving reasons, by means of a mounted messenger. This followed an alleged statement by a Franciscan from Schillingsfürst that a Catholic mass had been read in the chapel of the Order’s house. Lamprecht suspected this was the reason and denied that he had to accept orders from the imperial city council. The defendants then imposed a town and gate arrest on Lamprecht until he complied.
The plaintiff Ordensmeister argued that, as an imperial estate, he held all sovereign prerogatives by enfeoffment and, together with all Order houses in the German lands, was under the protection of Emperor and Empire; officials and other persons residing in the commanderies were exempt from the surrounding territories; the imperial city’s contractual criminal jurisdiction over the plaintiff’s officials, servants, and subjects did not give it territorial supremacy; the customary celebration of Catholic masses in the house chapel for persons living in the commandery was lawful; and the defendants should lift the arrest and be declared subject to the penalty threatened in the plaintiff’s privileges. The mayor and council replied that under the agreement of May 1605 they held universal jurisdiction over the Johanniterhof within the city walls and could arrest and punish within the Order house itself offenders not surrendered to them on demand. Lamprecht had already appeared at the town hall in mid-December 1752 in response to a summons, when he was accused of secretly having a Catholic mass read and thereby violating the imperial city’s ecclesiastical authority; he denied this. On a further summons he initially excused himself because of urgent business and promised to appear later, but then denied any obligation to comply with the summons. Instead of arresting him, the council had imposed only a town arrest. While the Komtur, Johann Pius Ignaz Freiherr von Bodman, was in Rothenburg, the arrest was temporarily lifted in mid-February 1753, and an amicable settlement of the dispute was agreed at the end of February 1753.
After the imperial city of Rothenburg was mediatized, the plaintiff applied to the Imperial Aulic Council because a Bavarian local commission had first sealed the estate of the late Komtur, Heinrich Ludwig Freiherr von Pfyffer, in late 1803, and then posted a land-homage patent inside the commandery.
Instances: 1. Imperial Aulic Council, 1753–1806 (1753–1804).
Printed “Diploma Cæsaræum Confirmationis Privilegiorum Equestris Ordinis S. Joannis Baptistæ Hierosolymitani. De Dato Viennæ 8.va Mensis Februarii 1748” (Q 5): confirmation by Emperor Franz I of the plaintiff Ordensmeister’s privileges in 1748, with an index summarizing their contents.
Witness statements before a notary, 1753 (Q 6).
Attachments to the exception pleading (Q 9): extracts from the “Historische und Rechtsbegründete Nachricht von dem Ursprung und LandStandschaft des Teutschen Hauses und LandCommende Marpurg” submitted by the Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel at the Perpetual Imperial Diet in Regensburg. These include the 1392 acknowledgment by the Johanniterkommende at Wiesenfeld to Landgrave Hermann of Hesse when its seat was temporarily moved to Frankenberg, and the same Landgrave’s 1392 record of an agreement between the commandery and the Cistercian convent of St Georgenberg concerning the parish at Frankenberg (Lit. M).
Attachments to the reply (Q 11): extracts from the Rothenburg Johanniterkommende’s records; certificates by Amtmann Johann Philipp Lamprecht and Capuchin Floribert of Comburg; and witness statements concerning frequent private Catholic masses in the Rothenburg house chapel and the Reichardsroth church, 1614–1753 (nos. 9–15); witness statement before the Rothenburg Johanniterkommende concerning a brawl, 1750 (no. 16).
File reports on a dispute over the purchase by Rothenburg citizen Johann Peter Ley of a hereditary-rent estate belonging to the Johanniterkommende, 1752–1753 (Q 15), with an extract from the commandery’s rent and land register (attachment no. 1); and on a brawl between servants and farmhands at the plaintiff’s farmyard at Reichardsroth in 1750 (Q 16), with a witness statement from Reichardsroth (1750), a certificate by Rothenburg town physician and medical licentiate Johann Nikolaus Raab and surgeon Johann Heinrich Schreiber concerning the injuries of farmhand Aegid Vogel of Reichardsroth, a list of his expenses, and the settlement oath of Georg Michael Döppert, son of the plaintiff’s tenant farmer Johann Michael Döppert of Reichardsroth (attachments nos. 3–6).
Opinions of an unidentified law faculty (Q 18, 19).
File report on the plaintiff’s claimed right to hold private worship in the Order house at Rothenburg (Q 20), with attachments (numbered in Arabic in the report and Roman numerals on the attachments): Emperor Leopold I’s rescript on Capuchins travelling through Rothenburg, 1668 (no. 4); correspondence of the Rothenburg mayors and council with the Comburg official at Gebsattel (1681), the Hohenlohe government chancery at Schillingsfürst (1721), various Johanniter administrators at Rothenburg (1693–1755), and the Generalrezeptor, Franz Nikolaus Freiherr von Forell (1756) (nos. 5, 10–13, 15–17, 20, 21, 23, 24, 30–34, 47, 49, 55–57, 61); extracts from Rothenburg court, interrogation, war-office, chancery, and council records—often including witness statements—and official reports, 1682–1756 (nos. 6, 7, 14, 18, 19, 25–29, 34b, 35–37, 40–42, 44–46, 48, 50–53, 59); instructions to the Rothenburg gate guard, 1721 (no. 22).
Letter from Generalrezeptor Gottfried Droste to the mayor and council of Rothenburg concerning collection of the Turkish tax, 1663 (Q 21).
Attachments to the rejoinder (Q 26): form of the fief oath sworn to the Johanniter administrator at Rothenburg, 1656 (no. 19); certificate by Franz Caspar Walther, Brandenburg-Ansbach councillor and chief district physician at Uffenheim, doctor of medicine, and surgeon Christian Schlichting concerning Aegid Vogel’s injuries, 1750 (no. 20); extract from a notarial instrument concerning the prioral visitation of the Rothenburg commandery ordered by the Grand Bailli, Generalrezeptor, and Statthalter, Johann Ignaz Wilhelm Freiherr von Gymnich, 1733 (no. 23).
Agreement between the Ordensmeister Weipert (von Rosenbach) and the mayors and council of Rothenburg, 1605 (Q 60).

Contents/insertions: Process beginning register: 1753.
